name: Hydrogen

etymology.detail: from Greek hydro + genes, 'water-former'

funFact: About three-quarters of all ordinary matter in the universe, by mass, is hydrogen.

name: Helium

etymology.detail: from Greek hēlios, the Sun, where it was spotted in 1868 before anyone found it on Earth

funFact: Helium was detected in the Sun’s spectrum 27 years before it was found on Earth.

name: Lithium

etymology.detail: from Greek lithos, 'stone'

funFact: Lithium is the lightest metal; it floats on water (and then reacts with it).

name: Beryllium

etymology.detail: named after the mineral beryl

funFact: Beryllium is nearly transparent to X-rays, so it’s used for X-ray tube windows.

name: Boron

etymology.detail: named after the mineral borax

funFact: Boron in borosilicate glass is why lab glassware survives sudden temperature changes.

name: Carbon

etymology.detail: from Latin carbo, 'charcoal'

funFact: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon — only the bonding pattern differs.

name: Nitrogen

etymology.detail: from Greek nitron + genes, 'niter-former'

funFact: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air you breathe.

name: Oxygen

etymology.detail: from Greek oxys + genes, 'acid-former' (a mistaken idea)

funFact: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth’s crust — nearly half its mass.

name: Fluorine

etymology.detail: named after the mineral fluorite, from Latin fluere, 'to flow'

funFact: Fluorine is the most electronegative element; it even forces noble gases like xenon to react.

name: Neon

etymology.detail: from Greek neos, 'new'

funFact: Only true neon signs glow red-orange; other colors use different gases or coatings.

name: Sodium

etymology.detail: from soda; the symbol comes from Latin natrium (natron)

funFact: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a butter knife.

name: Magnesium

etymology.detail: named after Magnesia, a district of Greece

funFact: Burning magnesium is so bright it was used in early camera flashes.

name: Aluminum

etymology.detail: from alum, Latin alumen

funFact: Aluminum was once pricier than gold; the Washington Monument is capped with it.

name: Silicon

etymology.detail: from Latin silex, 'flint'

funFact: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth’s crust, after oxygen.

name: Phosphorus

etymology.detail: from Greek phōsphoros, 'light-bearer'

funFact: Hennig Brand discovered phosphorus in 1669 by boiling down buckets of urine.

name: Sulfur

etymology.detail: from Latin sulpur

funFact: The “brimstone” of fire-and-brimstone is sulfur.

name: Chlorine

etymology.detail: from Greek chlōros, 'pale green'

funFact: Chlorine gas is a yellow-green color that gave the element its name.

name: Argon

etymology.detail: from Greek argos, 'lazy' or 'idle'

funFact: Argon makes up almost 1% of the air — far more than carbon dioxide.

name: Potassium

etymology.detail: from potash; the symbol comes from Latin kalium, via Arabic al-qalī, 'plant ashes'

funFact: Bananas are slightly radioactive because of their natural potassium-40.

name: Calcium

etymology.detail: from Latin calx, 'lime'

funFact: Calcium is the most abundant metal in the human body, mostly in bones and teeth.

name: Scandium

etymology.detail: named after Scandinavia (Latin Scandia)

funFact: Mendeleev predicted scandium as “eka-boron” before it was found.

name: Titanium

etymology.detail: named after the Titans of Greek mythology

funFact: Titanium is as strong as many steels at about half the weight.

name: Vanadium

etymology.detail: named after Vanadís, a Norse name for the goddess Freyja

funFact: Vanadium compounds come in a rainbow of colors, which is why it was named after a goddess of beauty.

name: Chromium

etymology.detail: from Greek chrōma, 'color'

funFact: Chromium gives rubies their red and emeralds their green.

name: Manganese

etymology.detail: from Magnesia, via Latin magnes (magnet)

funFact: About 90% of all manganese mined goes into making steel.

name: Iron

etymology.detail: from Anglo-Saxon īsern; the symbol comes from Latin ferrum

funFact: Iron is the most common element on Earth by mass, thanks to the planet’s core.

name: Cobalt

etymology.detail: from German Kobold, a mischievous mine goblin

funFact: Miners blamed “kobolds” for ore that gave off poison fumes instead of copper.

name: Nickel

etymology.detail: from German Kupfernickel, 'Old Nick’s (the devil’s) copper'

funFact: A US nickel coin is actually 75% copper.

name: Copper

etymology.detail: from Cyprus, via Latin cuprum (Cyprian metal)

funFact: The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper skin has oxidized.

name: Zinc

etymology.detail: from German Zink, perhaps from Zinke, 'prong'

funFact: Zinc coats (galvanizes) steel so it doesn’t rust.

name: Gallium

etymology.detail: named after Gallia, Latin for France

funFact: Gallium melts at 29.8 °C, so a gallium spoon melts in a cup of tea.

name: Germanium

etymology.detail: named after Germany

funFact: Mendeleev predicted germanium as “eka-silicon” 15 years before it was found.

name: Arsenic

etymology.detail: from Greek arsenikon, the yellow mineral orpiment

funFact: Arsenic was so popular with poisoners it was nicknamed “inheritance powder.”

name: Selenium

etymology.detail: from Greek selēnē, the Moon

funFact: Selenium conducts better in light, which made early photocopiers possible.

name: Bromine

etymology.detail: from Greek brōmos, 'stench'

funFact: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.

name: Krypton

etymology.detail: from Greek kryptos, 'hidden'

funFact: From 1960 to 1983 the meter was defined by a spectral line of krypton-86.

name: Rubidium

etymology.detail: from Latin rubidus, 'deep red', for its spectral lines

funFact: Rubidium melts at 39.3 °C — a hot day in Death Valley could melt it.

name: Strontium

etymology.detail: named after Strontian, a village in Scotland

funFact: Strontium salts give fireworks their crimson red.

name: Yttrium

etymology.detail: named after Ytterby, a village in Sweden

funFact: Yttrium-barium-copper oxide was the first superconductor above liquid-nitrogen temperature.

name: Zirconium

etymology.detail: named after the mineral zircon

funFact: Zircon crystals from Australia are over 4.4 billion years old — the oldest bits of Earth.

name: Niobium

etymology.detail: named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth

funFact: Niobium was named for Tantalus’s daughter because it was long confused with tantalum.

name: Molybdenum

etymology.detail: from Greek molybdos, 'lead', for the lead-like ore molybdenite

funFact: Molybdenum is a key part of the enzymes bacteria use to fix nitrogen.

name: Technetium

etymology.detail: from Greek technētos, 'artificial'

funFact: Technetium was the first element made artificially, in 1937.

name: Ruthenium

etymology.detail: named after Ruthenia, Latin for Russia

funFact: A dash of ruthenium makes platinum and palladium much harder.

name: Rhodium

etymology.detail: from Greek rhodon, 'rose', for its rose-colored salts

funFact: Rhodium is among the most expensive metals; it’s a key part of catalytic converters.

name: Palladium

etymology.detail: named after the asteroid Pallas, discovered a year earlier

funFact: Palladium can soak up 900 times its own volume of hydrogen.

name: Silver

etymology.detail: from Anglo-Saxon seolfor; the symbol comes from Latin argentum

funFact: Silver conducts electricity better than any other element.

name: Cadmium

etymology.detail: from Latin cadmia, the old name for calamine

funFact: Cadmium pigments give paint brilliant yellows and reds.

name: Indium

etymology.detail: named for the indigo line in its spectrum

funFact: Indium-tin oxide makes your touchscreen conductive and see-through.

name: Tin

etymology.detail: from Anglo-Saxon tin; the symbol comes from Latin stannum

funFact: Tin has 10 stable isotopes, more than any other element.

name: Antimony

etymology.detail: from Medieval Latin antimonium; the symbol comes from Latin stibium

funFact: Ancient Egyptians used antimony sulfide (stibnite) as black eyeliner.

name: Tellurium

etymology.detail: from Latin tellus, 'Earth'

funFact: People exposed to tellurium can get “tellurium breath,” which smells like garlic.

name: Iodine

etymology.detail: from Greek iōdēs, 'violet', for its purple vapor

funFact: Iodine is added to table salt to prevent goiter.

name: Xenon

etymology.detail: from Greek xenos, 'stranger'

funFact: Xenon was the first noble gas made to form a compound, in 1962.

name: Cesium

etymology.detail: from Latin caesius, 'sky blue', for its spectral lines

funFact: The second is defined by the vibrations of cesium-133 atoms.

name: Barium

etymology.detail: from Greek barys, 'heavy'

funFact: Patients drink a barium “milkshake” so their gut shows up on X-rays.

name: Lanthanum

etymology.detail: from Greek lanthanein, 'to lie hidden'

funFact: Each Toyota Prius battery holds roughly 10 kg of lanthanum.

name: Cerium

etymology.detail: named after the dwarf planet Ceres

funFact: Cerium is the “flint” in lighters — scrape it and it throws sparks.

name: Praseodymium

etymology.detail: from Greek prasios didymos, 'green twin'

funFact: Praseodymium tints welders’ goggles and gives glass a yellow-green color.

name: Neodymium

etymology.detail: from Greek neos didymos, 'new twin'

funFact: Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets you can buy.

name: Promethium

etymology.detail: named after Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods

funFact: Promethium is one of only two elements lighter than lead with no stable isotopes.

name: Samarium

etymology.detail: named after the mineral samarskite, which honors mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets

funFact: Samarskite made Samarsky-Bykhovets the first person to have an element (indirectly) named after them.

name: Europium

etymology.detail: named after Europe

funFact: Euro banknotes contain europium phosphors that glow under UV light.

name: Gadolinium

etymology.detail: named after Johan Gadolin, the Finnish chemist

funFact: Gadolinium is magnetic on a cool day and loses it on a warm one — its Curie point is about 20 °C.

name: Terbium

etymology.detail: named after Ytterby, a village in Sweden

funFact: Terbium’s green glow lights up phosphors in screens and lamps.

name: Dysprosium

etymology.detail: from Greek dysprositos, 'hard to get'

funFact: Lecoq de Boisbaudran needed more than 30 attempts to isolate dysprosium.

name: Holmium

etymology.detail: named after Holmia, Latin for Stockholm

funFact: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any element.

name: Erbium

etymology.detail: named after Ytterby, a village in Sweden

funFact: Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers boost the light signals that carry the internet across oceans.

name: Thulium

etymology.detail: named after Thule, a mythical land in the far north

funFact: Thulium is one of the rarest of the rare-earth elements.

name: Ytterbium

etymology.detail: named after Ytterby, a village in Sweden

funFact: Ytterbium atomic clocks are among the most precise ever built.

name: Lutetium

etymology.detail: named after Lutetia, the Latin name for Paris

funFact: Lutetium was the last stable rare-earth element to be discovered, in 1907.

name: Hafnium

etymology.detail: named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen

funFact: Hafnium is so good at absorbing neutrons it’s used in nuclear-sub control rods.

name: Tantalum

etymology.detail: named after Tantalus, who was tormented in the underworld

funFact: Most phones contain tantalum capacitors.

name: Tungsten

etymology.detail: from Swedish tung sten, 'heavy stone'; the symbol comes from wolframite

funFact: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, 3,422 °C.

name: Rhenium

etymology.detail: named after the Rhine river (Latin Rhenus)

funFact: Rhenium was the last stable element to be discovered, in 1925.

name: Osmium

etymology.detail: from Greek osmē, 'smell', for its pungent oxide

funFact: Osmium is the densest natural element: a liter of it weighs about 22.6 kg.

name: Iridium

etymology.detail: named after Iris, the rainbow, for its colorful salts

funFact: An iridium-rich layer in rocks worldwide marks the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.

name: Platinum

etymology.detail: from Spanish platina, 'little silver'

funFact: Platinum was once considered a nuisance that contaminated gold.

name: Gold

etymology.detail: from Anglo-Saxon gold; the symbol comes from Latin aurum

funFact: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 meters on a side.

name: Mercury

etymology.detail: named after the planet and god Mercury; the symbol comes from Latin hydrargyrum, 'water-silver'

funFact: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

name: Thallium

etymology.detail: from Greek thallos, 'green shoot', for its bright green spectral line

funFact: Thallium was a notorious poison because it’s tasteless and odorless.

name: Lead

etymology.detail: from Anglo-Saxon lead; the symbol comes from Latin plumbum

funFact: “Plumber” comes from plumbum, because Roman water pipes were made of lead.

name: Bismuth

etymology.detail: from German Wismut, of uncertain origin

funFact: Bismuth is technically radioactive, with a half-life a billion times the age of the universe.

name: Polonium

etymology.detail: named after Poland, Marie Curie’s homeland

funFact: Marie Curie named polonium for Poland, which was then partitioned and absent from the map.

name: Astatine

etymology.detail: from Greek astatos, 'unstable'

funFact: There’s less than a gram of astatine in Earth’s entire crust at any moment.

name: Radon

etymology.detail: from radium, which it comes from

funFact: Radon is the densest gaseous element, so it pools in basements.

name: Francium

etymology.detail: named after France

funFact: There’s only about 30 grams of francium in Earth’s crust at any moment.

name: Radium

etymology.detail: from Latin radius, 'ray'

funFact: Radium paint once made watch dials glow — and poisoned the women who painted them.

name: Actinium

etymology.detail: from Greek aktis, 'ray'

funFact: Actinium glows an eerie blue in the dark from its own radioactivity.

name: Thorium

etymology.detail: named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder

funFact: Thorium is about three times more abundant than uranium.

name: Protactinium

etymology.detail: from Greek prōtos + actinium, 'parent of actinium'

funFact: Protactinium is named “parent of actinium” because it decays into it.

name: Uranium

etymology.detail: named after the planet Uranus, discovered eight years earlier

funFact: Natural nuclear reactors ran in Oklo, Gabon, about 2 billion years ago.

name: Neptunium

etymology.detail: named after the planet Neptune, next out from Uranus

funFact: Neptunium was the first element heavier than uranium ever made.

name: Plutonium

etymology.detail: named after Pluto, next out from Neptune

funFact: Plutonium-238 powers spacecraft like Voyager and the Mars rovers.

name: Americium

etymology.detail: named after the Americas

funFact: Many household smoke detectors contain a tiny speck of americium-241.

name: Curium

etymology.detail: named after Marie and Pierre Curie

funFact: Curium was announced on a children’s radio quiz show in 1945.

name: Berkelium

etymology.detail: named after Berkeley, California

funFact: Berkelium was made by bombarding americium with alpha particles in 1949.

name: Californium

etymology.detail: named after California

funFact: Californium-252 gives off so many neutrons it’s used to kick-start nuclear reactors.

name: Einsteinium

etymology.detail: named after Albert Einstein

funFact: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test, in 1952.

name: Fermium

etymology.detail: named after Enrico Fermi

funFact: Fermium is the heaviest element that can be made by neutron bombardment.

name: Mendelevium

etymology.detail: named after Dmitri Mendeleev

funFact: Mendelevium was the first element made one atom at a time — 17 atoms in 1955.

name: Nobelium

etymology.detail: named after Alfred Nobel

funFact: Nobelium’s discovery was disputed for decades by labs in Sweden, the US and the USSR.

name: Lawrencium

etymology.detail: named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron

funFact: Lawrencium is named after the inventor of the cyclotron, the machine that made it possible.

name: Rutherfordium

etymology.detail: named after Ernest Rutherford

funFact: Rutherfordium was claimed by both Soviet and American labs during the Cold War.

name: Dubnium

etymology.detail: named after Dubna, home of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research

funFact: Dubnium went by at least three other names during the “Transfermium Wars.”

name: Seaborgium

etymology.detail: named after Glenn T. Seaborg

funFact: Seaborg joked his mail could be addressed in elements: seaborgium, lawrencium, berkelium, californium, americium.

name: Bohrium

etymology.detail: named after Niels Bohr

funFact: Only a few dozen atoms of bohrium have ever been made.

name: Hassium

etymology.detail: named after Hesse, the German state where it was made

funFact: Hassium is predicted to be the densest element of all, about 41 g/cm³.

name: Meitnerium

etymology.detail: named after Lise Meitner

funFact: Lise Meitner helped explain nuclear fission but was left out of the Nobel Prize for it.

name: Darmstadtium

etymology.detail: named after Darmstadt, Germany

funFact: Darmstadtium was first made in 1994 by smashing nickel into lead.

name: Roentgenium

etymology.detail: named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays

funFact: Roentgenium sits below gold but only a handful of its atoms have ever existed.

name: Copernicium

etymology.detail: named after Nicolaus Copernicus

funFact: Copernicium was named on Copernicus’s 537th birthday.

name: Nihonium

etymology.detail: named after Japan (Nihon, 'land of the rising sun')

funFact: Nihonium was the first element discovered in Asia.

name: Flerovium

etymology.detail: named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions, itself named for Georgy Flerov

funFact: Flerovium might be a volatile metal, or even a gas, at room temperature.

name: Moscovium

etymology.detail: named after the Moscow region

funFact: Moscovium atoms survive for less than a second.

name: Livermorium

etymology.detail: named after Livermore, California, home of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory

funFact: Livermorium is named after the lab that teamed up with Dubna to make it.

name: Tennessine

etymology.detail: named after Tennessee, home of Oak Ridge National Laboratory

funFact: Tennessine got its “-ine” ending because it sits in the halogen column.

name: Oganesson

etymology.detail: named after Yuri Oganessian

funFact: Oganesson is the heaviest element ever made, and one of only two named after a living person.
